messages.text: What are the main findings of this paper?

messages.short_answer: The paper reports that 10 non-expert participants explored prompts opportunistically rather than systematically, and struggled in ways echoing end-user programming and interactive machine learning. Human-to-human instruction expectations and a tendency to overgeneralize from few examples were key barriers.

sections.title: Core findings from the abstract
sections.text: The authors state that probe participants explored prompt designs opportunistically, not systematically, and that expectations from human-to-human instruction and a tendency to overgeneralize were barriers to effective prompt design. The introduction adds that participants struggled to make robust, systematic progress.

sections.title: Specific behaviours reported in the study
sections.text: According to PaperLens's overview of the user study pages, most participants declared success after a single successful instance, relied on local testing, and rarely used error labeling or systematic testing. Zero participants used the systematic prompt testing interface in the reported study (ov-8, ov-11). Participants also favored 'do not' phrasing over the more effective 'do' phrasing.

sections.title: Implications the authors draw
sections.text: The authors discuss implications for designing end-user-facing LLM tools, for education to improve LLM and prompt literacy, and for further research. Their proposals include tool support for cause-and-effect exploration between prompt changes and conversational changes, and training that encourages systematic testing.

sections.title: Relevance to your user study
sections.text: Your study of how non-experts write prompts overlaps closely with these findings, so the reported behaviours (opportunistic testing, human-like phrasing, overgeneralization) could be useful as hypotheses or coding categories. Note that the participant pool was small (10) and skewed toward STEM professionals and graduate students, and the authors state it is not representative.

sources.text: These pages from the user study section of 'Why Johnny Can't Prompt' describe how ten non-expert participants iteratively designed prompts for a recipe chatbot (CarlaBot) using the BotDesigner tool, with interviewer advice given during the session and analysis via affinity diagrams and service blueprints. The authors report that participants took an ad hoc, opportunistic approach, starting from observed chatbot errors such as humorlessness, overly complicated statements, skipping steps, and undesired explanations, then editing the preamble instructions, often by pattern matching existing text. Participants usually declared success after a single successful instance and relied on local testing rather than systematic testing, with limited use of error labeling. The main findings attribute struggles to over-generalization from single observations and to mental models of the system rooted in human-human interaction; the authors note as a limitation that interviewer advice was not uniform across participants.

These pages discuss a user study of prompt design with a chatbot tool called BotDesigner, focusing on how participants used error labeling and systematic testing. Participants largely stopped labeling errors once they realized the labels were not used by the system, and none used the systematic prompt testing interface, instead declaring victory after a single successful change. The authors describe this as premature victory declaration, similar to overconfident end-user programmers, and note that some professional programmers were more concerned about generalizability. The pages also cover participants struggling to explain why prompts worked or failed across contexts, and a finding that participants favored 'do not' phrasing over the more effective 'do' phrasing, with the authors linking this to early childhood education literature.

These pages discuss design implications and limitations from a study of end-user prompt design for LLM-backed chatbots (BotDesigner). They argue that users need more examples of an error class before feeling confident it is resolved, and that tools should make successful examples discoverable and support exploring cause-and-effect between prompt changes and conversational changes. The authors suggest designs that hide the instruction-like nature of prompting or have the app perform socially violating work itself, and note that seamful design may make the app's non-human nature visible. Stated limitations include a small, academic early-adopter sample, limited time for prompt design, and the need for future work on other populations, non-chatbot domains, and the role of social expectations (CASA).

These pages discuss a study of how end-users prompt LLM-based chatbots (GPT-3), focusing on mismatches between users' expectations and LLM behavior. Participants were surprised that trivial prompt changes, such as rephrasing or adding a negated 'Don't' instruction, could produce dramatically different outputs, and that plain behavioral descriptions were not always followed. The authors note that participants could rarely explain why the model behaved as it did, given the black-box nature of LLMs. The discussion then offers implications for training and education, including encouraging users to collect more data and perform systematic testing, and suggests searchable example repositories and explanations of instruction time horizons. The pages end by raising design opportunities, such as heuristics for how much data or how many conversations are needed for robustness testing.

These pages describe the participant table and the interview protocol for a study where participants used the BotDesigner tool to improve a baseline chatbot so it could mimic a conversational style seen in a cooking video. Participants (ten people with varied professions and LLM knowledge) were shown an episode of Back to Back Chef and a transcript with color-coded highlights of humor, analogies, concept simplification, and step confirmation. They had up to one hour to prompt the bot toward these behaviors, with the researchers observing approach rather than final quality, and offering prompt suggestions only after participants got stuck for several minutes. Researchers also reminded participants of labeling, systematic error testing, and edit/replay functions when relevant. Figure 3 shows the opening turns of the expert-amateur cooking transcript used as the target.

messages.text: Which of their study methods could I use for my user study?

messages.short_answer: The paper's clearest reusable methods are a design-probe study with about 10 participants who lack prompt-design experience, a think-aloud protocol, video transcription with exploratory analysis, and a note of where interviewers intervened. Its own limitations (small, non-representative sample and inconsistent advice across participants) are worth designing around in your study.

sections.title: Core study design the authors used
sections.text: The authors used BotDesigner as a design probe and observed 10 participants without substantial prompt design experience completing a chatbot design task. Participants were asked to think aloud, and the team transcribed all videos and did exploratory data analysis.

sections.title: Protocol elements you could adapt
sections.text: The think-aloud sessions, full video transcription, and noting of struggles and interviewer interventions could transfer directly to a study of non-expert prompt writing. A design probe like BotDesigner could also give your participants a common, controlled tool, which you would need to choose or build for your own research question.

sections.title: Sample size and scope
sections.text: The authors chose 10 participants in line with formative usability testing, aiming to find the first, easy-to-find problems rather than full coverage. They also state that their pool, skewed towards STEM professionals and graduate students, is not representative of the population at large.

sections.title: Consistency of interventions
sections.text: The authors offered prompt suggestions during sessions but did not vary this advice intentionally, so participants did not all receive the same advice or in the same order. They describe this as a limitation of their approach, so a stricter intervention protocol would be needed in your study if you offer hints.

retrieved.text: Why Johnny Can’t Prompt: How Non-AI Experts Try (and Fail) to Design LLM Prompts J.D. Zamfrescu-Pereira zamf@berkeley.edu UC Berkeley Berkeley, CA, USA Bjoern Hartmann bjoern@eecs.berkeley.edu UC Berkeley Berkeley, CA, USA ABSTRACT Pre-trained large language models (“LLMs”) like GPT-3 can engage in fuent, multi-turn instruction-taking out-of-the-box, making them attractive materials for designing natural language interactions. Using natural language to steer LLM outputs (“prompting”) has emerged as an important design technique potentially accessible to non-AI-experts. Crafting efective prompts can be challenging, however, and prompt-based interactions are brittle. Here, we explore whether non-AI-experts can successfully engage in “end-user prompt engineering” using a design probe—a prototype LLM-based chatbot design tool supporting development and systematic evaluation of prompting strategies. Ultimately, our probe participants explored prompt designs opportunistically, not systematically, and struggled in ways echoing end-user programming systems and interactive machine learning systems.

Ultimately, our probe participants explored prompt designs opportunistically, not systematically, and struggled in ways echoing end-user programming systems and interactive machine learning systems. Expectations stemming from human-to-human instructional experiences, and a tendency to overgeneralize, were barriers to efective prompt design. These fndings have implications for non-AI-expert-facing LLM-based tool design and for improving LLM-and-prompt literacy among programmers and the public, and present opportunities for further research. CCS CONCEPTS • Human-centered computing → Empirical studies in interaction design; • Computing methodologies → Natural language processing. KEYWORDS language models, end-users, design tools ACM Reference Format: J.D. Zamfrescu-Pereira, Richmond Wong, Bjoern Hartmann, and Qian Yang. 2023. Why Johnny Can’t Prompt: How Non-AI Experts Try (and Fail) to Design LLM Prompts. In Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’23), April 23–28, 2023, Hamburg, Germany. ACM, New York, NY, USA, 21 pages.

This excitement around LLMs and prompting is propelling a rapidly growing set of LLM-powered applications [23] and prompt design tools [3, 20, 32]. Yet despite widespread excitement, surprisingly little is known about how non-experts intuitively approach designing prompts with LLM-and-prompt-based tools, and how efective they are in doing so. While prompting LLMs can appear efortless, designing efective prompting strategies requires identifying the contexts in which these LLMs’ errors arise, devising prompting strategies to overcome them, and systematically assessing those strategies’ efectiveness. These tasks fall on so-called “prompt engineers”— the designers, domain experts, and any other end-user or professional attempting to improve an LLM’s output—and are challenging tasks even for LLM experts, as well as topics of ongoing research in Natural Language Processing (NLP) [7, 30, 42]. Prompt design tools to date have focused on supporting professional programmers [45] and NLP practitioners [42], rather than non-AI experts, non-programmers, and other potential end-users of these systems.

2.2 Known Challenges in Prompt Design While prompting can appear as easy as instructing a human, crafting efective and generalizable prompt strategies is a challenging task. How a prompt or a prompt strategy directly impacts model outputs, and how prompts modify LLMs’ billions of parameters during re-training, are both active areas of NLP research [30, 42]. Moreover, established prompt design workfows do not yet exist. Even for NLP experts, prompt engineering requires extensive trial and error, iteratively experimenting and assessing the efects of various prompt strategies on concrete input-output pairs, before assessing them more systematically on large datasets. That said, ongoing NLP research does ofer some hints toward efective prompt design strategies. Notably, these prompt strategies are efective in improving LLMs’ performance over a range of NLP tasks and conversational contexts; it remains unclear to what extent these strategies can improve any particular conversational interactions or contexts.

Examples of this advice include “try reframing that ‘do not’ statement into a positive statement, say what it is you want the bot to say, not what you don’t want it to say” or “have you considered copying some of the Carla-Lizzie transcript directly into the preamble?” We did not intentionally vary this advice across participants; however, due to the unpredictable nature of which errors participants chose to focus on, not all participants received the same advice or advice in the same order, a limitation of our approach. Analysis & Evaluation. We asked participants to think aloud, then engaged in exploratory data analysis, transcribing all videos and observing what prompt design approaches participants attempted, and noting when participants appeared to struggle and where interviewers intervened.

Using this tool as a design probe, we observed how 10 participants without substantial prompt design experience executed a chatbot design task using BotDesigner, to explore a few diferent pieces of this larger question. Our fndings suggest that, while end-users can explore prompt designs opportunistically, they struggle to make robust, systematic progress. Their struggles echo many well-known struggles observed in end-user programming systems (EUPS) and non-expect users of interactive machine learning (iML) systems. Additional barriers to efective prompt design stem from limited conceptions of LLMs’ prompt understanding and execution abilities and their understandable inclinations to design prompts that resemble human-to-human instructions. We discuss these observations’ implications for designing efective end-user-facing LLM-based design tools, implications for education that improves LLM-andprompt literacy among programmers and the general public, and opportunities for further research. This paper makes three contributions.

They had up to one hour to prompt the bot toward these behaviors, with the researchers observing approach rather than final quality, and offering prompt suggestions only after participants got stuck for several minutes. Why Johnny Can’t Prompt: How Non-AI Experts Try (and Fail) to Design LLM Prompts J.D. Zamfrescu-Pereira zamf@berkeley.edu UC Berkeley Berkeley, CA, USA Bjoern Hartmann bjoern@eecs.berkeley.edu UC Berkeley Berkeley, CA, USA ABSTRACT Pre-trained large language models (“LLMs”) like GPT-3 can engage in fuent, multi-turn instruction-taking out-of-the-box, making them attractive materials for designing natural language interactions. Using natural language to steer LLM outputs (“prompting”) has emerged as an important design technique potentially accessible to non-AI-experts. Crafting efective prompts can be challenging, however, and prompt-based interactions are brittle. Here, we explore whether non-AI-experts can successfully engage in “end-user prompt engineering” using a design probe—a prototype LLM-based chatbot design tool supporting development and systematic evaluation of prompting strategies. Ultimately, our probe participants explored prompt designs opportunistically, not systematically, and struggled in ways echoing end-user programming systems and interactive machine learning systems.

This excitement around LLMs and prompting is propelling a rapidly growing set of LLM-powered applications [23] and prompt design tools [3, 20, 32]. Yet despite widespread excitement, surprisingly little is known about how non-experts intuitively approach designing prompts with LLM-and-prompt-based tools, and how efective they are in doing so. While prompting LLMs can appear efortless, designing efective prompting strategies requires identifying the contexts in which these LLMs’ errors arise, devising prompting strategies to overcome them, and systematically assessing those strategies’ efectiveness. These tasks fall on so-called “prompt engineers”— the designers, domain experts, and any other end-user or professional attempting to improve an LLM’s output—and are challenging tasks even for LLM experts, as well as topics of ongoing research in Natural Language Processing (NLP) [7, 30, 42]. Prompt design tools to date have focused on supporting professional programmers [45] and NLP practitioners [42], rather than non-AI experts, non-programmers, and other potential end-users of these systems.

Why Johnny Can’t Prompt CHI ’23, April 23–28, 2023, Hamburg, Germany After this initial phase, again in the interest of observing subsequent behavior, we would ofer suggestions for prompts to try that were in line with the research around prompt design. Examples of this advice include “try reframing that ‘do not’ statement into a positive statement, say what it is you want the bot to say, not what you don’t want it to say” or “have you considered copying some of the Carla-Lizzie transcript directly into the preamble?” We did not intentionally vary this advice across participants; however, due to the unpredictable nature of which errors participants chose to focus on, not all participants received the same advice or advice in the same order, a limitation of our approach. Analysis & Evaluation. We asked participants to think aloud, then engaged in exploratory data analysis, transcribing all videos and observing what prompt design approaches participants attempted, and noting when participants appeared to struggle and where interviewers intervened.

Participants. All participants ( = 10) had little to no experience with prompt design; none had substantial prior experience 2Regression tests, in the context of software engineering and in the sense we intend here, are tests that verify that any new changes to a system do not reintroduce previously-resolved errors (called regressions). working with LLMs. We recruited participants with varying levels of programming and chatbot design experience. Recall that our focus here is understanding end-users in the domain of prompt design; experience in chatbot design was thus not considered grounds for exclusion. Our sample size was chosen in line with prior work around formative testing for usability [19, 43]: our goal is to explore the frst, “easy-to-fnd” problems users encounter when engaged in our task, and our experience with a pilot user suggested that problem discoverability was likely to be high. Our participant pool, skewed towards professionals and graduate students in STEM-related felds, is not representative of the population at large.

2.2 Known Challenges in Prompt Design While prompting can appear as easy as instructing a human, crafting efective and generalizable prompt strategies is a challenging task. How a prompt or a prompt strategy directly impacts model outputs, and how prompts modify LLMs’ billions of parameters during re-training, are both active areas of NLP research [30, 42]. Moreover, established prompt design workfows do not yet exist. Even for NLP experts, prompt engineering requires extensive trial and error, iteratively experimenting and assessing the efects of various prompt strategies on concrete input-output pairs, before assessing them more systematically on large datasets. That said, ongoing NLP research does ofer some hints toward efective prompt design strategies. Notably, these prompt strategies are efective in improving LLMs’ performance over a range of NLP tasks and conversational contexts; it remains unclear to what extent these strategies can improve any particular conversational interactions or contexts.

Using this tool as a design probe, we observed how 10 participants without substantial prompt design experience executed a chatbot design task using BotDesigner, to explore a few diferent pieces of this larger question. Our fndings suggest that, while end-users can explore prompt designs opportunistically, they struggle to make robust, systematic progress. Their struggles echo many well-known struggles observed in end-user programming systems (EUPS) and non-expect users of interactive machine learning (iML) systems. Additional barriers to efective prompt design stem from limited conceptions of LLMs’ prompt understanding and execution abilities and their understandable inclinations to design prompts that resemble human-to-human instructions. We discuss these observations’ implications for designing efective end-user-facing LLM-based design tools, implications for education that improves LLM-andprompt literacy among programmers and the general public, and opportunities for further research. This paper makes three contributions.

(This strategy is under-investigated in text generation.) Little research has investigated how non-experts conduct prompt engineering intuitively or the challenges they encounter. One rare exception is a CHI’22 workshop paper “How to prompt?” [14], where Dang et al. conducted a focus group with HCI researchers and identifed an initial set of challenges they encountered in prompting. These challenges include “the lack of guidance in trial and error, ” “poor representation of tasks and efects, ” and “computational costs and ethical concerns. ” In prompting text-to-image models such as DALL·E, an adjacent area to prompting LLMs, Liu et al. describe a study with artists, identifying emergent strategies for prototyping prompts, such as “try multiple generations to get a representative idea of what prompts return” and “focus on keywords rather than the phrasings of the prompt” [31]. This paper builds upon this emergent line of research and aims to deepen these understandings. 2.3 Non-Expert Prompt Design Tools Arguably, the most widely used prompt design tool among nonexperts remains the OpenAI Playground, a “plain text” input box that triggers GPT-3 to predict text completions.

3 METHOD: DESIGN PROBE In this work, we aim to understand how non-experts intuitively approach designing robust prompts, and whether and how they struggle in doing so. We want to dive deep into what those struggles reveal about people’s assumptions and understanding of promptbased systems in order to inform how end-user-facing prompt design tools might best support their users. We chose to investigate these questions in the context of designing instructional chatbots—chatbots that walk users through an activity (e.g., cooking a recipe, fxing a wif connection) while answering user questions and engaging in social conversation as needed. Chatbot tasks are sufciently open-ended that they open the door to a wide variety of types of problems and prompt-based solution approaches. Instructional chatbots represent a common chatbot use case (e.g., customer service bots), and their constituent tasks are some of the tasks that GPT-3 peforms more efectively out-of-the-box.

Systematic testing and robust prompt design—designing prompts that work across many users and many conversations—are by defnition impossible if the user only ever engages in a single conversation, even continuously updated. That said, for some contexts non-robust prompt design can be appropriate: chatbots intended for a single user who is also the designer do not necessarily need to be robust. A second major opportunity stems from the fact that most of the prompt design approaches participants tried before receiving any guidance (see §3.3 for details regarding this guidance) had some efect—enough for participants to feel that they could, in fact, afect chatbot output with prompt changes—but participants hit dead ends that incurred interviewer intervention more frequently than we expected. A searchable repository of examples, such as The DALL·E 2 Prompt Book [37], could help users overcome the “design”, “selection”, and “use” barriers that often led to the aforementioned dead ends.

Throughout this section, prompt text is set in monospace font, while spoken participant comments and user/bot dialog messages are “quoted. ” 4.1 Overview: Non-Experts’ Approach to Prompt Design In our open-ended prompt design task, participants almost exclusively took an ad hoc, opportunistic approach to prompt exploration. From that starting point, the typical fow is: (1) Participants start an example conversation as the baseline chatbot’s “user” partner, continuing until the bot issues an utterance that the participant deems in error.
